MESSAGE:
Hi. I'm off to Lisbon next week for a three-day work trip, my first time in Portugal, and I want to travel carry-on only this time, after the airline lost my case in the spring.

Could you suggest three things to do in Lisbon on a free evening? And how do I say "thank you" in Portuguese? Is it different depending on who's saying it? And is tipping expected in restaurants there, or is that more of an American thing?

My wheeled bag measures 56 × 36 × 23 cm including the wheels and handle, and packed it weighs 9 kg. Will it meet the carry-on limit?

Also, recommend a packing approach: rolling or folding for work shirts? I need a short out-of-office message that's professional but not stiff, since most of my contacts are clients rather than colleagues. And what's a good colour for a luggage tag so it's easy to spot? I'm flying back on the Friday evening, straight after a full day of meetings, so anything that makes the return journey less stressful is welcome.

Thanks a lot.

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest three things to do in Lisbon in the evening
2. Explain how to say 'thank you' in Portuguese and whether it varies by speaker
3. Say whether tipping is expected in Lisbon restaurants
4. Determine whether a 56 x 36 x 23 cm, 9 kg bag meets the carry-on limit  KEY: Missing datum: the airline (and fare type) is not stated, and carry-on size/weight limits vary by airline and fare, so this cannot be confirmed. Should ask which airline/fare and illustrate: under a common 55 x 40 x 20 cm limit the bag fails (56 > 55 length, 23 > 20 depth); under a 56 x 45 x 25 cm limit it fits; weight limits range roughly 7-10 kg, so 9 kg may exceed a 7 or 8 kg limit.
5. Recommend rolling vs folding shirts
6. Write a short out-of-office message
7. Suggest a luggage tag colour

ANSWER:
Here's everything in order.

## Your bag: probably not, depending on the airline

Cabin limits vary by airline, and your bag is just over the most common size.

| Airline (typical standard cabin bag) | Size limit | Weight limit | Your 56 × 36 × 23 cm, 9 kg |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAP Air Portugal | 55 × 40 × 20 | 8 kg | ❌ too deep, too heavy |
| Ryanair (priority / paid) | 55 × 40 × 20 | 10 kg | ❌ too deep |
| Lufthansa group | 55 × 40 × 23 | 8 kg | ❌ 1 cm long, 1 kg heavy |
| British Airways | 56 × 45 × 25 | 23 kg | ✅ |
| easyJet (large cabin bag, paid) | 56 × 45 × 25 | 15 kg | ✅ |

The 23 cm depth is the main problem, because many airlines cap depth at 20 cm. Check the exact limit on your booking, since policies change and can differ by fare. If your airline is a 20 cm one, a soft holdall or backpack around 40 × 30 × 20 cm will compress to fit and avoid paying at the gate. Tell me the airline and I can be more specific.

## "Thank you"

- **Obrigado** (oh-bree-GAH-doo) if you're a man
- **Obrigada** (oh-bree-GAH-dah) if you're a woman

The ending matches the *speaker's* gender, not the listener's. **Muito obrigado/a** means "thank you very much."

## Tipping

Tipping isn't expected the way it is in the US.
- **Restaurants:** rounding up or leaving 5–10% for good service is appreciated but optional. Card machines often have no tip option, so leave coins if you want to tip.
- **Cafés and bars:** small change at most.
- **The couvert:** bread, olives or cheese may be put on the table when you sit down. They aren't free; you're charged if you eat them. You can send them back without any awkwardness.

## Three evening ideas

1. **Sunset at a miradouro (viewpoint).** Senhora do Monte has the widest view. São Pedro de Alcântara is easy to reach and close to Bairro Alto and Príncipe Real for dinner afterwards.
2. **Fado in Alfama or Mouraria.** Fado is Portugal's traditional melancholic song. A small tasca (tavern) is more atmospheric than a big dinner-show venue. Book ahead, and expect silence during songs.
3. **Dinner and a wander in Príncipe Real or Chiado.** Both are good for food and are lively but less chaotic than Bairro Alto. If you're short on time, Time Out Market by Cais do Sodré offers lots of choice under one roof.

## Packing work shirts

**Fold** work shirts and **roll** everything else.
- Button the shirts and fold them around a stiff folder or piece of card. Stack them collar to tail, then put them in a packing folder or flat pouch.
- Roll knits, T-shirts and casual clothes to fill gaps.
- On arrival, hang the shirts in the bathroom while you shower and the steam will release most creases. Most business hotels can also lend you an iron.

## Out-of-office message

> Thank you for your email. I'm travelling for work from [Wednesday date] to [Friday date], with limited access to email. I'll reply when I'm back on [Monday date].
>
> If your message is urgent, please contact [Name] at [email / phone], who will be glad to help.
>
> Best regards,
> [Your name]

Set it to run until Monday morning. You won't want to answer clients on Friday night.

## Luggage tag colour

Pick something that stands out against a sea of black bags: **neon orange, lime green, or hot pink**. Since you're carry-on only, the tag matters most if your bag is gate-checked on a full flight. Add a bright strap or ribbon to the handle so it's easy to spot in the overhead bins too.

## Making Friday less stressful

- **Pack Thursday night.** On Friday, check out in the morning and either leave your bag at the hotel or bring it to the meetings.
- **Check in online** and keep your boarding pass on your phone. With carry-on only, you can go straight to security.
- **Check your terminal.** Lisbon airport has two, and Terminal 2 (mostly low-cost carriers) is reached by a shuttle bus from Terminal 1, so allow extra time.
- **Leave buffer time.** The airport is only 20–30 minutes from the centre by metro or taxi. But Friday-evening traffic and security queues can be slow, so aim to arrive about 2 hours before departure.
- **Keep your liquids bag and charger on top** so security is quick and your phone isn't flat when you need your boarding pass.
- **Change into comfortable clothes** before leaving if you can, and keep a snack handy in case your meetings run into dinner.

Have a great trip, and *boa viagem!*
